newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi prince buys stake in TWA.
newsitem.headline: Saudi prince buys stake in TWA.

text.p: The billionaire nephew of Saudi Arabia's King Fahd said Wednesday he purchased a 5 percent stake in Trans World Airlines, which earlier this week revealed deeper-than-expected losses.
Saudi Arabia's Prince al-Waleed bin Talal has previously invested in banks, hotels, chain stores, and theme parks.
Financial analysts said the TWA purchase fell within the prince's business strategy of buying stakes in ailing companies and trying to put them back on their feet.
The prince's TWA stake is not as big as his other global investments, but his office in Riyadh said his latest buy -- the first in the airline industry -- was a new investment trend.

TWA, based in St. Louis, said the prince told the carrier he has no plans to purchase additional shares in the company at this point. It said the prince called TWA Chairman Gerald Gitner and said he had purchased about 5 percent, or 2,088,000 shares, of the company's common stock.
TWA said the prince also said he is hopeful that management will succeed in its effort of bringing the airline to long-term profitability.
TWA said Tuesday it had a loss of $258.6 million on revenues of $803.3 million in the fourth quarter of last year. In the year-earlier period, it lost $27.8 million on revenues of $804.6 million.
TWA reported a 1996 loss of $284.8 million, including special charges of $85.9 million, on revenues of $3.55 billion. In 1995, the airline lost $227.5 million on revenues of $3.32 billion.

"I have a big portfolio and this is part of diversification," said the prince, reached by telephone from his Riyadh office. He would not elaborate on his latest acquisition, but a statement issued by his office said it was for investment purposes.

Prince al-Waleed -- who turned 40 on March 7 -- is a grandson of Saudi Arabia's founder Ibn Saud. People who know him say he started with a relatively small amount of money from his father and is now one of the wealthiest and most powerful business moguls in the oil-rich kingdom.

Surrounded by a close circle of advisers, he controls an international portfolio that includes a bank, an investment firm, a supermarket chain, a broadcasting operation, and huge property holdings including the Fairmont and Four Seasons hotel chains.

He has helped bail out the Euro Disney theme park near Paris and Canary Wharf in London's Docklands. He also bought stakes of former Italian Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi's television and advertising business Mediaset.
Earlier this year he bought Paris' luxury George V hotel.

In a most unlikely scenario for a prince from a conservative Moslem country, Prince Al-Waleed last year signed a deal with U.S. popstar Michael Jackson setting up Kingdom Entertainment to cooperate on concerts, films, television, fun parks and hotels.
His holding company is called Kingdom Establishment. People who know him say he is never far from a telephone, even when he goes to the desert or the Mediterranean.
"I've got a rule of thumb: Anything that's worth $4 billion and costs $1 billion -- buy it!" he once said.
The prince is a 1979 graduate in sciences from California's Menlo Park College. He also received a master's degree in social science at the University of Syracuse.
The prince is the chairman of the United Saudi Commercial Bank, one of Saudi Arabia's smaller banks, which turned into one of its most dynamic when he took over in 1988.

He first showed his Midas touch in 1991 when he bought 14.88 percent of Citicorp at a bargain-basement price of about $800 million. The deal made him the largest shareholder of the bank. He also invested $100 million in upmarket retailer Saks Fifth Avenue.
Earlier this month the prince said he was spending $500 million to build a commercial complex in Riyadh to house a Four Seasons Hotel.
